Laboratory study of the PFRC-2’s initial plasma densiﬁcation stages S.A. Cohen*,1 E.S. Evans,1 L. David,1 P. Jandovitz,1 S. P. Vinoth,1 E. Palmerduca,1 C.P.S. Swanson,1 G. Jusino-Gonzalez,1 and A. Dogariu2

1)Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, 08543 USA 2)Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering Department, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, 08543 and Department of Aerospace Engineering, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, 77843 USA

(*Electronic mail: scohen@pppl.gov)

(Dated: 24 September 2023)

Initial plasma densiﬁcation by odd-parity rotating magnetic ﬁelds (RMFo) applied to the linear magnetized PFRC-2 device with ﬁll gases at pressures near 1 mTorr proceeds through two phases, a slow one, characterized by a rise time τslow ∼100 µs, followed by fast one, characterized by τ fast ∼10 µs. The transition from slow to fast occurs at a lineintegral-averaged electron density, tne, near 2 × 1011 cm−3, independent of magnetic ﬁeld. Over most of the range of experimental parameters investigated, as the PFRC-2 axial magnetic-ﬁeld strength is increased, RMFo power decreased, gas ﬁll pressure lowered, or lower atomic-mass (AMU) ﬁll-gas used, the duration of the slow phase lengthened from 50 µs to longer than 10 ms after the RMFo power began. The post-fast-phase maximum ne increases with the ﬁll-gas AMU, exceeding 5 × 1013 cm−3 for Ar. The slow phase is consistent with atomic physics processes and ﬁeld-parallel sound-speed losses. The fast phase may be explained by improved axial conﬁnement, possibly augmented by radial or axial contraction of the plasma. Another possible explanation, a large increase in electron temperature, is inconsistent with X-ray emission. The ne behavior is discussed in relation to the E to H transition.

I. INTRODUCTION

Field-reversed-conﬁguration (FRC) plasmas are characterized by high β (ratio of plasma energy density to magnetic ﬁeld energy density), quasi-toroidal geometry, toroidal current, zero toroidal magnetic ﬁeld and a high degree of selforganization.1–3 Research into FRCs is strongly motivated by their potential as fusion reactors for electricity generation or spacecraft propulsion and as materials-processing devices. Forming FRCs is essential to these studies and applications. FRC plasmas have been created by numerous methods: θ-pinch ﬁeld reversal;4,5 plasmoid merging;6,7 laser ionization;8 rotating magnetic ﬁelds (RMF);9–11 and energetic beam injection.12,13 Several of the methods exhibit µs-timescale ﬁeld-line tearing and reconnection at X-points on a developing separatrix, initially well removed from the major axis. Particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations of FRC formation by odd-parity rotating magnetic ﬁelds (RMFo) show a different behavior – the FRC grows from a region near the major axis, centered on the axial midplane.14

In this paper, experiments that explore the initial plasma densiﬁcation phase on the PFRC-2 device by RMFo heating are described. This is a step in the development of RMFo FRC-formation scenarios needed as higher magnetic ﬁeld, larger-radius devices – culminating in FRC reactors – are considered. RMFo heating which makes FRCs with high atomicmass-number (AMU) ﬁll gas at low magnetic ﬁeld strengths, may not form FRC plasmas at the higher magnetic ﬁelds and with lower AMU ﬁll gases needed in fusion reactors. MHD modeling of even-parity RMF (RMFe) have concentrated on RMFe penetration into existing magnetized plasma columns having ﬁxed plasma density and temperature, nominally equal to those in the FRC’s ﬁnal state.9,15,16 They have not investigated the evolution of plasma parameters, other than the driven current. A result of these studies is that RMFe, with frequency ωRMF << ωpe, the electron plasma frequency,

penetrates a short distance into the plasma,17 the collisionless skin depth, δ, until the bulk electrons co-rotate azimuthally with the RMFe; at that time full penetration rapidly ensues. A heuristic explanation is that the rotating magnetic ﬁeld does not change with time in the moving frame of co-rotating electrons, hence shielding of magnetic ﬁelds does not occur. In apparent conﬂict with this idea is the observation18 that RMFe penetrated only to the FRC’s null-point line. Without full penetration, the fullest beneﬁts predicted for RMF, such as ion and electron heating and efﬁcient current drive,19–21 may not be obtained. The subjects of anomalous skin depths and mechanisms responsible for ﬁeld penetration have been, for decades, topics of intense research. The experiments described herein study the application of RMFo power to low density seed plasma, focusing on the density increase in the evolving plasma. Because the seed plasma is low density, the RMFo is initially fully penetrated. Some of the physical processes involved are identical to classical DC and RF breakdown studies.22 Noteworthy novel features are: a) a low-density target seed plasma already exists with the RMFo fully penetrates; b) ωRMF is far below ωpe and the electron cyclotron frequency, ωce; c) ωRMF is slightly above ωci, the ion cyclotron frequency; d) axial boundary conditions – potentials on surfaces – exist and are in the range -3 to +3 kV; and, e) due to the PFRC-2 and antenna geometries, wave, capacitive, and inductive effects may be important. Section II describes the PFRC-2 device and its diagnostics. Section III starts with a presentation of the variation of the density-rise behavior with machine parameters, providing an introduction to correlations between density rise rate, emitted visible light and X-rays, absorbed power, atomic mass of the ﬁll gas, maximum density, etc. Discussion of the data, evaluation of the relevance of a small fast electron population, comparison to the E- to H-mode discharge transition,17 and a regression analysis of the data are presented in section IV.

II. APPARATUS A schematic of the PFRC-2 is shown in Figure 1a). Four 25-cm-ID coaxial magnet coil sets and two coaxial 1.8-cm- ID nozzle coils, positioned symmetrically about the Lexan center-cell vacuum-vessel’s (CC) axial midplane, generate a mirror magnetic ﬁeld. The midplane on-axis vacuum ﬁeld, B(0,0), is up to 400 G. Several near-axis magnetic ﬁeld lines are shown in Figure 1a). Figure 1b) shows a typical on-axis magnetic ﬁeld strength proﬁle. The ﬁeld proﬁle changes when the plasma β is high. Eight electrically ﬂoating ∼16-cm-ID, coaxial, BN-clad copper rings, each embedded with high temperature superconducting (HTS) tape, are in the CC and are called ﬂux conservers, FCs. Their inductive current decay time is 5 ms at room temperature and 1 s at LN2 temperature. Low density seed plasma (light blue), the target plasma for the RMFo, is shown decorating near-axis ﬁeld lines. The ﬁll gas may be bled into the source end cell (SEC) or CC. The desired pressure is maintained by balancing this gas input with turbo pump exhaust from each section. With a ﬁllgas pressure in the SEC of 1 mTorr, the pressure in the CC, pcc, is near 0.5 mTorr and 10−5 T in the far end cell (FEC). The base pressure in the system is below 10−6 T, falling below 10−8 T with LN2 cryopumping in the CC. Without cryopumping, RGA measurements in the FEC show the dominant impurity gas to be H2O, at a partial pressure typically near 1% of the ﬁll gas. With cryopumping, the total pressure of all impurity gases is less than 0.1%. At the SEC’s far end is a double-saddle antenna wrapped around a 3.8-cm-ID Pyrex pipe, Figure 1c). The antenna is the inductor in a T-type tank circuit driven by a 27-MHz RF ampliﬁer that provides power, Psp, up to 800 W. This antenna creates the seed plasma whose density increases with Psp. One axial boundary is an electrically biasable plasmafacing steel cup at the antenna end of the Pyrex pipe. The bore of a nozzle coil – a 1.8-cm-ID, 4-cm-long stainless-steel tube – connects the SEC to the CC. The other end of the CC is connected to the FEC through an identical nozzle coil. The FEC houses the other axial boundary, an electrically biasable movable Ta paddle. High-impedance high-voltage probes are connected to the cup in the SEC and to the Ta paddle in the FEC. With a seed-plasma source power of Psp ∼50 W and a SEC

H2 ﬁll pressure 0.5-3 mTorr, typical plasma parameters are: electron temperature, Te ∼5 eV; electron density, ne ∼109

cm−3; and plasma ﬂoating potential, φf = 20 Volts. The seed plasma also contains a minority (0.1-1%) electron population characterized by a Te in the range 0.2-2 keV. This minority population has a higher Te at higher Psp and lower pcc. Four RMFo antenna sections, each of 31-cm axial length, are 3 cm outside the CC vessel and centered about the axial midplane. (The antenna section pairs are called north/south, N/S, and top/bottom, T/B.) Grounded Faraday shields are between each antenna section and the Lexan vessel. Figure 1a) shows two of the four, T/B. The antenna is powered by a 200- kW RF ampliﬁer (1-30 MHz) capable of 50-ms operation at full power and longer at lower power. The ampliﬁer’s output is split, half going to a tank circuit connected to T/B antenna sections and the other half going to a tank circuit that feeds the N/S antenna sections. The power to the two tanks is phaseshifted 90◦such that the magnetic ﬁeld (usually) rotates in the ion-diamagnetic-drift direction. The Q of the unloaded RMFo antennae plus tank circuits is about 75. At ωRMF = (2π)4 MHz, this results in 25±5 µs for 95% of the ultimate current to circulate in the antenna. The RMF system’s frequency source has an intrinsic 25 ± 5 µs delay before the start of the RMF power, PRMF. The RMFo system is usually operated with a 1% duty factor, resulting in ∼3600 discharges/hr. The forward (Pf ) and reﬂected power (Pr) are measured at the power splitter. Also measured is the power absorbed by the plasma (Pa). Typically, Pa ∼0.2 − 0.5Pf , in agreement with our modeling that a sizeable fraction of the RMFo power is dissipated in the tank circuit. All the data in this paper were at Pf less than 110 kW and at RMFo frequencies of 1.8, 4.3, 6, or 8 MHz. Typically, the RMFo’s peak on-axis vacuum magnetic ﬁeld was 1-10% of B(0,0). The diagnostics include: 1) a 170-GHz heterodyne interferometer that views across a plasma diameter 11 cm from the axial midplane. It provides a line-integral electron density, ¯ne, converted to a volumetric density under the assumption of a uniform density across the full FC diameter, 16 cm; 2) electrical potential measurements on the steel cup and Ta paddle; 3) a femtosecond TALIF system,23 providing Ho and Kro density measurements in the CC; 4) a near-midplaneviewing scannable monochromator to measure line emission;

III. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

For the data in Figure 2, the RMFo power is turned on at t = 0 and applied for 6 ms: Pf = 60 kW; Psp = 100 W; and B(0,0) = 220 G. The ﬁll gas was Ar at pcc = 0.53 mTorr. A 0.3- ms-duration hydrogen puff into the CC was begun at 2.05 ms, raising the pressure between discharges to 0.67 mTorr. Figure 2a) is the electron density, an average of 113 discharges. From t = 0.1 to 0.6 ms, ne shows a slow rise and then transitions to a more rapid rise. (Unless noted, τD is measured from t = 0, i.e., no ∼50 µs correction is made for the Q of the tank circuit and intrinsic delay of the RMFo system.) τD displays a shot-to-shot jitter, a point to which we shall shortly return. Figure 2b) shows the Hβ emission for a single discharge — mis-alignment of the trigger time is seen in the H-β rise and fall — and Figure 2c) shows <Pa> vs time for the N/S antenna set, averaged over 800 discharges. For these discharges, Pa prior to τD was about 65% of Pa after τD. Pa prior to τD is a greater fraction of Pa after τD at lower RMFo frequency than at higher frequency. Lower frequency RMFo required higher power for the rapid densiﬁcation stage to be reached.

A. Early time evolution of plasma density

The electron density shown in Figure 2 is the average of 113 plasma discharges, hence hides possible shot-to-shot variation, including those caused by jitter and plasma motion. The peak electron density would be higher if the plasma diameter was smaller than the FC ID or the plasma had an axial or radial proﬁle, e.g., hollow. Soon we shall present data supporting a

smaller radius for the post-start-up plasma. Nevertheless, unless speciﬁcally noted, we assume the plasma diameter to be 16 cm throughout this paper. Figure 3a) shows, with higher time resolution, the densi- ﬁcation phase for a single 8-ms-duration discharge that has a large initial 35-kHz m=1 rotational mode. The factor-of-2 amplitude variation in line-average density is consistent with a ×1.8 reduction of the plasma column’s radius, with an equal increase in peak plasma density, assuming the plasma edge is bounded by the FC. Also shown are the density smoothed with a co-moving 5-µs window and the derivative of that smoothed signal. The initiation time of the rapid densiﬁcation may be deﬁned as when the derivative exceeds a threshold, in this case set at 5 × 1016 cm−3s−1. The effect of using this criterion can be seen in Figure 3b) which compares this derivativethreshold criterion with the RMFo-trigger-time criterion for synchronizing the time evolution of ne of many discharges. A derivative- or density-threshold criterion reduces the jitter, revealing successive stages of slow (here t = 0 to 0.35 ms) then rapid (t = 0.35 to 0.37 ms) density growth.

FIG. 3. a) Initial density rise of a single RMFo discharge. The green curve is its derivative. b) Density rise averaged over 420 RMFo discharges. Blue: average synchronized with RMFo start (trigger) time (normal average); Red: average synchronized (aligned average) with the initial spike in the derivative.

The semi-log scale of Figure 4 shows this more clearly. The density rise is characterized by two exponentials. Figure 4 (top): a slow rise from 50 to 120−190 µs with τslow ∼35−50 µs to a density near 1.5×1011 cm−3, followed by a more rapid rise, τ fast ∼5−7 µs, to ne = 2.5×1012 cm−3. Higher RMFo power shortens τD, τslow and τfast and increases the ﬁnal density. It is seen in this ﬁgure that an increase in magnetic ﬁeld strength increases the duration of the slow rise period and increases τslow, even though the power has been increased; similarly, τ fast is lengthened as B(0,0) is increased.

F. Ho formation The time- and spatially resolved Ho density was measured with a femtosecond TALIF system.23 Figure 14 shows, with 10 µs resolution, the early time evolution of the Ho density near the PFRC-2’s major axis and midplane: PRMF = 81 kW;

H2 ﬁll gas; and pcc = 0.5 mTorr. These data were accumulated over 103 discharges and synchronized by the “normal" method. Similar to the ne behavior previously shown, a slow rise in Ho density is seen through the ﬁrst 0.25 ms, followed by a more rapid rise over the next 0.25 ms. The H-β light lags the the Ho density. The Ho spatial proﬁle was measured to be nearly constant across the plasma column’s diameter, a point now discussed.

FIG. 14. Ho density (black) and H-β (red) emission (arb) vs time. After 1 ms, the Ho density decreases, falling to 2×1011 cm−3 at 3 ms. 20210413

Ho is formed in the PFRC-2 with a Franck-Condon energy near 2 eV, primarily by electron-impact dissociation of H+ 2 . Electron-impact dissociation of H2 is about 10% as important. Electron-impact ionization of H2 to H+ 2 proceeds at 1/3 the rate. Loss of Ho from the plasma volume proceeds by ionization or transport to the walls. At Te = 100 eV, EH0 = 2 eV and ne = 2×1012 cm−3, the ionization life time is 15 µs; the radial transit time is somewhat longer, ∼30 µs. That the Ho

density is about 1/3 of the electron density, their creation is by the same process, and assuming that Ho is lost on impacting the walls; at that time the Ho conﬁnement times would be 3× longer than the net, > 30 µs. Later in the discharge the Ho

density falls a factor of four, hence the electron conﬁnement time would grow four times longer, > 120 µs. That the proﬁle of the Ho density is independent of radius is consistent with the plasma density, electron temperature, and an Ho Franck- Condon energy. For high-AMU inert gas plasmas, the neutral atomic density falls as the plasma density grows and the mean-free-path shortens; the above method for ﬁnding the particle conﬁnement time is not applicable but particle balance arguments may be used.

H. RMFo resonant frequency during densiﬁcation

Herein we show the behavior of the resonant frequency of the RMFo system prior to, during and subsequent to the two densiﬁcation stages. The example shown is for H2 ﬁll gas, P f ∼100 kW and B(0,0) = 100 G. The RMFo system is ﬁrst tuned with no plasma to ﬁnd that frequency resulting in the least percentage of reﬂected power, typically below 1%, see Figure 19. In this case the resonant frequency (into vacuum), fres,v, was 1.7952±0.0001 MHz. During the ﬂat-top period of the discharge, that is, subsequent to the fast densiﬁcation, the resonant frequency, fres,p, increased to 1.7978±0.0001 MHz.

IV. DISCUSSION

Many others have studied steady-state plasma parameters in RF-heated magnetized discharges, typically at considerably higher frequency (30 MHz), lower magnetic ﬁeld (20 G), lower RF power density (×100) and higher ratio of RF magnetic ﬁeld to steady-state magnetic ﬁeld.26 Similary, many have studied the penetration of RF and RMF ﬁelds9,10,15 into plasmas, some as functions of β, others as functions of polarization. FRC plasmas have been the target of such studies, with RF penetration being the focus. Fruchtman et al.27,28

concluded that either Whistler waves or lower hybrid drift turbulence could explain the penetration. A recent study showed that n = 0,1 modes29 could explain the penetration. In contrast, the studies described herein are of the time evolution of the plasma formation phase in different parameter regimes. Notably, the RMFo ﬁeld starts fully embedded in the plasma and, interpreting the data in Figure 21 in the same manner as Cohen et al.,11 the RMFo ﬁeld is excluded from the region r < 2.5 cm during the rapid densiﬁcation phase. The data presented show that τD may grow by orders-ofmagnitude depending on B(0,0), Psp, pcc, P f , and AMU. Even if τD remains ﬁnite, practical problems may occur in reactorscale devices. Two examples are: a high reﬂected PRMF may result in damage to elements of the RMF power system; and the energy required to form the FRC may exceed the energystorage-system’s capacity. A variety of conditions were shown to result in shorter τD. These include: higher P f ; lower initial magnetic ﬁeld; higher Psp; optimized pcc; smaller plasma ﬁnal radius; and higher AMU ﬁll gas. Though a qualitative understanding of the increase in τD with increasing B(0,0) and decreasing pcc is obtained from the relatively weak dependence30 of the anomalous skin depth31 on magnetic ﬁeld — δa ∝B0.4 — and even weaker on collisionality, quantitative predictions require fully kinetic simulations because of the need to include electron scattering on ion and neutrals, the proﬁles of B and ne, their time evolution, and the polarization of the RMFo. Quantitative numerical simulations of the time evolution of the plasma parameters will be presented in subsequent papers. Further concerning the need for detailed simulations, the initial phases of a discharge’s density behavior differ when the RMFo rotates in the “wrong" direction (counter, Cntr), that opposite to what is considered correct (Co) for driving electron current.9,10,32

For Cntr RMFo, P f levels are required to be about 3× higher for the rapid densiﬁcation phase to occur. At P f levels comparable to when densiﬁcation ﬁrst occurs with Co rotation, the CC plasma density drops to about 1/2 of that provided by the seed plasma, a phenomenon called “RF pump out" by earlier researchers.33 As Pf is increased, a slow density rise phase occurs for about 1 ms; the density then saturates. When P f is sufﬁciently high, rapid densiﬁcation ﬁnally occurs and saturates at about the same peak density as with Co rotation. The density measured in these discharges ﬂuctuates ± 75% in a time scale of 0.3 ms. Fluid simulations of RMFe would not show electron current drive for the Cntr rotation direction.32 In contrast, Hamiltonian simulation do, if a ﬁeld-reversed proﬁle has been assumed.20

Based on the above data, a few scenarios for providing adequate τD in reactors are: a ramp-up of magnetic ﬁeld during start up; initially a high-AMU ﬁll gas, being replaced by fusion-fuel species, e.g., D, after an FRC has formed, a motivation for the experiments illustrated in Figure 2; smaller seed-plasma radius; higher density seed plasma (Figure 15), such as by a helicon plasma or by higher Psp; or by employing a non-RMF method of FRC formation, such as those noted in Section I. Additionally, the larger radius of reactors may allow a shorter τD, as soon described. Understanding the existing data will help choose the proper method for achieving the desired τD in larger, higher ﬁeld FRC devices.

A. The role of the seed plasma’s fast electrons One important question concerns the process by which the RMFo antennae couple power to the seed plasma. The slow time, τslow, is consistent with ionization by bulk electron impact: τslow = (no < σv >i)−1 ∼50 µs for < σv >i at Te typical of the bulk seed plasma electrons, 5-7 eV, where no is the neutral density and < σv >i is the ionization rate coefﬁcient. A similar estimate shows that the minority fast electron population present in the capacitive-discharge-formed seed plasma25 plays little role, if any, in the slow densiﬁcation stage. The fast electron density is typically 0.1% of the bulk seed plasma density while the ionization rate for hydrogen only increases ×50 when Te is raised from 5 to 500 eV. Amplifying this conclusion is the immediate loss of the seed plasma’s fast electrons when RMFo is applied, as indicated by the X-ray signal (Figure 11). Supporting the expulsion of fast electrons by the RMFo is the observation of the negative spike in Vpaddle at the beginning of the slow densityrise phase (Figure 12). This indicates a burst of energetic electrons impacting it. The charge deposited on the paddle approximately equals the fast electron content measured in the CC by the X-ray diagnostics. This conclusion is reinforced by measurements of the density rise when RMFo is applied with no seed plasma. At the seed plasma’s initially low density, the RMFo fully penetrates the CC plasma column: c/ωpe = δ > 10 cm. The RMFo induces electric ﬁelds in the seed plasma in directions both parallel (E||) and perpendicular (E⊥) to B. The extent of the electron motion parallel to E is determined by the RMFo period, the length of the PFRC-2 and its antenna, the RMFogenerated E||, and the local strength of the total B. For BRMF = 10−3 T, ωRMF = 2.5×107/s, and an antenna half-length La = 0.2 m, Faraday’s Law gives E|| ∼(0.5ωRMFBRMFLa) = 2500 V/m, causing electrons a maximum energy gain of ∼500 eV and an average energy of ∼160 eV for this population. At lower ωRMF and higher RMFo power, energetic electrons would be more readily lost axially to the cup or paddle during each half of an RMFo cycle. E⊥from the RMFo will cause electron drift motion in the low-β plasma with drift energy of order 1 eV, too low to affect ionization. Collisions with neutrals may result in ionization and reduce an electron’s energy and loss rate: νe,n/ωRMF ∼1 for the present RMFo frequency, 1.8 MHz, electron energy near 50 eV, and Ar gas at 1 mTorr. This collisionality-to-frequency ratio is close to that in the classical Paschen regime. The τD

An interpretation based on the decrease in X-ray emission from the CC immediately upon application of RMFo and by the rapid fall of Vcup, 200 V in Figure 12, is that the seed plasma’s minority fast electron population is accelerated by the RMFo’s E|| into the loss cone. The bulk electrons are similarly accelerated along the ﬁeld line. The mean-free-path for ionization, λi, for fast electrons at 160 eV and 1 mTorr Ar is 30 cm. At the energy of the fast electrons, the characteristic time of density rise would be ∼1 µs, much faster than observed, another support for our conclusion that fast electrons are not important in the formation process. Restating this point: the fast electron population is so small that it contributes little to the densiﬁcation stage. With the conclusion that fast electrons in the seed plasma contribute little to the density rise opens the possibility to use higher density seed plasma, such as helicon plasmas, which contain few fast electrons.

B. The transition, τD The transition from slow to fast density-rise stages occurs at nearly constant density, tne ∼2 × 1011 cm−3, independent of B(0,0) and pcc, Figure 5. The lack of sensitivity to B(0,0) argues against β effects as the cause of this particular value of

tne. As indicated in Figure 15, the duration of the slow phase decreases as Psp increases, however, τslow does not change. That τD shortens with increasing Psp is consistent with a constant tne, independent of the seed plasma density. At tne = 2 × 1011 cm−3, δ has decreased to 1.1 cm, see Figure 19, neglecting the predicted effects of B(0,0) and pcc.30

A common criterion for the transition from E- to H-mode is that the skin depth falls to near the plasma dimension.34,35 If the same occurred for an FRC reactor of the PFRC type, tne would be near 109 cm−3, greatly alleviating the concern.

Contributing factors to the divergence from the power law, evident for Ar at R > 300, may be the non-algebraic behaviors of the anomalous skin depth, the ionization rate, and the electron collisionality, particularly how it affects the parallel thermal conduction. If a reactor of the PFRC-type followed the scaling shown in Figure 23, the 100-fold increase in the regression-ﬁt parameter leads to τD exceeding 1 s. A far larger τD would occur if the trend followed the diverging data points, those at R > 300. Higher power RMFo allows greater energy losses than the lower power seed plasma source, an important contributor the higher density achieved with RMFo. (The ﬁfty-fold electron temperature increases seen are even more important to con- ﬁnement questions.) That the maximum initial density increases with AMU argues in favor of the relevance of ion sound speed losses in the axial direction, in addition to electron thermal conduction. Moreover, based on plasma radial proﬁles, losses in the radial direction are estimated to be low. Assuming Te = 50 eV, the maximum initial density with RMFo is consistent with < β >= 1 for Ar at the observed ne = 2×1013 cm−3 and B(0,0) = 200 G. Higher electron temperatures and more rapid sound speed losses are expected for H2 discharges because of their lower radiation losses. Hence lower maximum densities would be obtained at <β >= 1 with hydrogen ﬁll gas. Increasing the ﬁll pressure ﬁrst causes a shorter mean-freepath for ionization, therefore a shorter τD, see Figure 8. As in RF Paschen breakdown studies, above a certain pressure, electrons have too short a mean-free-path to gain sufﬁcient energy from E|| for ionization and the breakdown process is hindered, as shown by the increase in τD for pcc > 1-2 mTorr. As noted before, elastic collisions of electrons with neutrals decreases the parallel energy losses, contributing to a shorter τD. In RF Paschen models and because of the ratio of the RF period to the electron transit time, the effective length of the CC may be many times longer than the device length and surface effects are unimportant for breakdown, e.g., plasma densiﬁcation in our case. The pressure at which τD is minimum, see Figure 8, is 0.5-2 mTorr, depending on B(0,0). Consistent with the RMF frequency and machine size, about 10 electron oscillations occur along the PFRC-2’s length before an electron is lost axially when the PFRC-2 is heated by 100 kW of RMFo. Then pcc def f = 10−3Torr×102cm ×10 = 1 Torr cm, where def f is the effective length of the plasma, yielding a value of pcc def f close to that obtained in DC Paschen experiments. A large def f is similar to that reported for ECR breakdown36 in smaller devices, though here pccdef f is 10 times lower, expected to be due to the lower frequency of RMFo. Based on the above, we suggest a two-step process fol-

lowed by a plateau. In step 1, the entire slow density-rise phase, δa greatly exceeds rc (FC radius), the RMFo electric ﬁeld fully penetrates the tenuous plasma and accelerates all electrons equally, resulting in Pa ∝ne. The energy conﬁnement time (from power balance) is short, ∼100 ns, the transit time of 100 eV electrons along B. (At ne < 2×1011 cm−3 and no < 1013 cm−3, electrons with energy > 5 eV can free stream to the axial boundaries.) The energy conﬁnement may be improved with a increase of neutral density (pcc), an effect that reverses as radiation losses climb. The absorbed power increases when δa ∼rc, as it does at the transition to an H-mode. Step 2 is during rapid densityrise phase. Here τD depends strongly on B, implying a β effect. At <β> = 0.5, ﬁeld lines close and energy conﬁnement improves. An FRC forms. Improved conﬁnement is necessary to explain the factor of 100 density rise. A density plateau develops when <β> ∼1. Consistent with this, X-ray brightness increases as ne falls during a discharge, that is, Te grows in conjunction with ne falling such that neTe is constant. Secondary electrons are emitted by ion impact on the SEC steel cup. These seed-plasma electrons, accelerated to several hundred eV by the sheath, deposit their energy in the plasma column, causing ionization there both directly and by the warmed bulk electrons. Nevertheless, capacitive discharges lose ∼80% of their energy to their negative self-biased electrode by ion impacts. Moreover, because Psp < 0.5 kW and the secondary electron yield < 0.1, the secondary electrons contribute little to the power balance during the RMFo-heated stage.

V. CONCLUSION

Through laboratory experiments on the RMFo-heated PFRC-2 device, we have identiﬁed 3 characteristic times for the initial density rise, τslow, τ fast and τD. The slow density rise phase is explicable to ionization events at low Te, ca. 5-7 eV. Transition to the more rapid density rise requires better power absorption and, more importantly, improved particle and energy conﬁnement. Improved power absorption would occur – consistent with the idea from E- to H-mode transitions – as the skin depth decreases to less than the plasma radius. Better conﬁnement would follow, caused by increased β, ﬁeld line closure, and the formation of an FRC. Over the range B(0,0) = 50 - 400 G, the electron density at which a transition from slow to fast density rise occurs is insensitive to the applied magnetic ﬁeld, implying that the skin depth is a more important factor than β. The maximum density observed increases with the AMU of the ﬁll gas. Methods to achieve the high density state by RMFo in larger, higher ﬁeld devices were described.
